Rulings

A ruling is a recorded decision: a rule for many words, or a choice on one word where we depart from a dictionary or a source. Each of the 23 below gives its reasons with the evidence, its date, who made it and its status: current, provisional (awaiting a further check) or withdrawn. When a ruling changes, its history says how and why. The general rules behind them are on How we decide.

Spelling · Vowel length · Usage · Word choices

Spelling

Clipped -ne keeps an apostrophe

current 29 October 2026 · Jack

Write satin', vīn', ain', audīn', scīn', vidēn', with the vowel as long or short as in the base word.

The apostrophe marks the lost e of -ne. There is no compensatory lengthening: satin' keeps the short a of satis, audīn' the long ī of audīs. A following est keeps its e (satin' est, Ter. Ph. 210).

Consonantal i is written j

current 29 October 2026 · Jack

Write consonantal i as j in all Latin, quotations included: jam, ejus, major, conjungō, Joannēs.

The lexicon follows the spelling of the Theodōrus et pater readers, which use the j of Lewis & Short. Between vowels j was pronounced double, so the syllable before it is heavy while its vowel is short (rejice scans heavy although re- is short, Verg. Ecl. 3.96): major, ejus, pejus therefore carry no macron, while long prefixes keep theirs (dējectus, prōjēcit). The letter stays i where it is a vowel: in the interjection iō, in forms of eō (iērunt, adiērunt), in superior, interior, Plēiades, in Iūlus where Vergil makes it three syllables, and after qu and gu (quiēs, reliquiae). Citation labels keep each dictionary’s own headword. Search treats i and j alike.

Forms: jam, ejus, major, conjungō, adjuvō, Joannēs

  • 26 October 2026: Adopted for the readers.
  • 29 October 2026: Applied to the whole lexicon.

oiei keeps its i

provisional 8 November 2026 · Claude; awaiting Jack’s review

Write oiei as Lewis & Short prints it, not ojei.

It is unclear whether the i’s of this interjection are vowels or consonants, so the j rule is not applied. The form also depends on the edition: the Perseus text of Terence does not print oiei at the places Lewis & Short cites. For a plain “ouch”, au is the better-attested word.

Forms: oiei

Vowel length

Macrons are spelling

current October 2026 · Jack

Mark every long vowel, fully and consistently, as part of the spelling.

Macrons are treated like the accents of French: part of the word, not an aid for beginners. Short vowels are left plain, and a heavy syllable is not by itself a long vowel. Hidden quantities, long vowels in syllables already heavy by position, are marked too (rēctus, cīnctus).

ōlla with a long o

current October 2026 · Latinitas review

Write ōlla, ōllae with a long o.

ōlla is the later form of aula (Festus: aulās antīquī dīcēbant, quās nōs dīcimus ōllās), and an o that comes from au is long, as in cōda beside cauda and plōstrum beside plaustrum. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked; the quantity is hidden by the double l.

Forms: ōlla, ōllae

Cited in: saucepan

jentāculum with a short e

current 23 October 2026 · Lexicon review

Write jentāculum and jentō with a short e.

Lewis & Short leaves the e unmarked, and no authority we follow marks it long.

Which authority settles a vowel

current 28 October 2026 · Jack

Lewis & Short first; Bennett for hidden quantities that Lewis & Short leaves unmarked; de Vaan wherever he explicitly discusses the vowel.

Lewis & Short marks most quantities but leaves many hidden ones blank, and Bennett’s study of hidden quantity fills those gaps. De Vaan’s Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008) is the most recent of the three, so where he discusses a vowel he takes precedence (sāriō). Where the authorities conflict, the entry says which one we followed.

Short vowels before gn

current 29 October 2026 · Jack

A vowel before gn is short unless its stem is long: magnus, signum, lignum, ignis, dignus, pugnus, pugna, but rēgnum (from rēx), stāgnum, sēgnis, abiēgnus.

This follows Bennett, Buck and Allen against the rule reported by Priscian that every vowel before gn is long. It is a deliberate exception to the precedence of de Vaan, whose pūgnus, pūgna (s.v. pungō) are not followed.

frūstrā with a long u

current 30 October 2026 · Jack

Write frūstrā; frustum, “a piece”, is a different word, with a short u.

De Vaan (s.v. fraus) derives it from *fraud-tro-, and Bennett cites an apex (CIL VI 20370): both give a long u.

narrō with a short a

current 30 October 2026 · Jack

Write narrō, narrāre, not nārrō.

De Vaan (s.v. gnārus) derives the verb from *nārāre, shortened by the littera-rule, which Weiss calls the “narro rule”; de Vaan comes first where he discusses a vowel. Bennett’s nārrō rests on a single apex, NÁRREM in the Lyon tablet (CIL XIII 1668), on a syllable already long by position; in those inscriptions only about three apices in four stand on long vowels.

Perfect subjunctive -erīs, future perfect -eris

current 30 October 2026 · Jack

The perfect subjunctive has a long ī (nē dīxerīs), the future perfect a short i (sī vēneris). A form that could be either is left short.

Bennett, and Allen and Greenough (§169.d), give the perfect subjunctive the long ī of the old optative. A clause drawn into a subjunctive clause counts as subjunctive (cum jūdicāverīs, Ps. 50:6 in Jerome’s psalter from the Hebrew); a general condition with a timeless present, or the polite grātum fēceris, stays short.

cedo with short vowels

current 7 November 2026 · Jack

Cedo! “give it here” has a short e and a short final o, and its plural is cette.

Lewis & Short marks it cĕdo and lists it apart from cēdō, cēdere “go, give way”. It is an old imperative, from -ce and the root of dō.

caccabus: a short a and a double c

provisional 8 November 2026 · Claude; awaiting Jack’s review

Write caccabus (also cacabus), not Lewis & Short’s cācabus.

The word is Greek κάκκαβος, with a short α and a double κ. Varro writes caccabum (cited by Lewis & Short), and Statius scans albōrum calicum atque caccabōrum (Silv. 4.9.45) with a heavy first syllable, which the double c explains. Lewis & Short’s cācabus marks that heavy syllable as a long vowel. Our Comenius quotation table still follows Lewis & Short.

Forms: caccabus, cacabus

Cited in: cooking pot

fortasse with a short final e

current 8 November 2026 · Jack

Write fortasse, not Lewis & Short’s fortassē.

Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel. De Vaan (2008: 236, s.v. fors) speaks of the word’s “short final vowel”, and verse proves it: in Catullus 85.1, Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam fortasse requīris, the fifth foot, -tasse re-, must be a dactyl, so the e is short. Horace scans it the same way (S. 1.3.20, 1.6.98).

Forms: fortasse

Cited in: perhaps

lutra with a short u

current 8 November 2026 · Jack

Write lutra, not Lewis & Short’s lūtra.

Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel, and its only etymological note, luō, has a short one. De Vaan (2008: 355) prints lutra and Proto-Italic *udrā-, from PIE *ud-ro- “of the water”, with the short u of Sanskrit udrá- and Greek ὕδρος. The long vowel of Lithuanian ūdra and Bulgarian видра comes from a Balto-Slavic lengthening (Winter’s law), which says nothing about Latin. Italian and Portuguese lontra and French loutre continue a short u; a long ū would have given u, as in luna and lune. The word occurs only in prose (Varro, Pliny), so verse cannot decide.

Forms: lutra, lutra marīna

Cited in: backstroke

mixtus with a short i

provisional 8 November 2026 · Claude; awaiting Jack’s review

Write mixtus, mixtōria, permixta without a macron on the i.

Traupman marks the i long, but Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked in mixtum, and de Vaan (2008: 382–383) prints mixtum, mixtūra with a short i, explaining mixtum as syncopated from *mixitum. Spanish mestizo and French métis, from Late Latin mixtīcius, also continue a short i. Bennett has not been checked yet.

Forms: mixtus, mixtōria, permixtus

Usage

dēbeō is for duty

current 27 October 2026 · Jack

dēbeō with an infinitive expresses duty or obligation; for what simply had to happen, use necesse est.

Lewis & Short: in classical prose it is always used of moral necessity.

Word choices

opus caementīcium for concrete

current 29 October 2026 · Lexicon review

Concrete is opus caementīcium, not Traupman’s concrētum.

After Vitruvius’s caementīcius.

furcilla for the fork

current 29 October 2026 · Lexicon review

The table fork is furcilla, not fuscinula.

furcilla is a classical word (Varro, Cicero) whose table-fork sense is modern (Traupman 71). fuscinula occurs only in the Vulgate.

exedra for the sitting room

current 29 October 2026 · Lexicon review

The sitting room is exedra, not sessōrium.

exedra is a room for sitting and conversation in Vitruvius and Cicero (Traupman 125). The ancient senses of sessōrium are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”.

Turning a tap on and off

current 29 October 2026 · Jack

On: epitonium vertere. Off: epitonium claudere, or aquam sistere.

The verb is Varro’s (epitoniīs versīs, R. 3.5.16); compare Vergil’s sistere aquam fluviīs (A. 4.489). Traupman’s versāre and reversāre are not used: reversāre is late Latin. In narration, forms that do not sound the same in present and perfect are preferred (epitoniō versō, not vertit).

linteum and mantēle

current 29 October 2026 · Jack

The bath towel is linteum and the hand towel mantēle; a tablecloth is also linteum.

mantēle is the hand towel in Varro (L. 6.85) and Vergil (A. 1.702), and Martial uses lintea of a tablecloth (villōsa tegant tibi lintea citrum, 14.138). Traupman’s gausapina is classically a frieze coat, and manutergium is found only in Isidore.

gelātum for ice cream

current 7 November 2026 · Jack

Ice cream is gelātum; Traupman’s congelidum crēmum and Morgan–Owens’s glaciēs dulcis are given as alternatives.

Antiquity had no ice cream to name, so the choice is between modern coinages. This one is the easiest to say, and it has modern precedent (Helfer; Vox Latina, both cited by the Neo-Latin Lexicon).
